title: Understand an unfamiliar codebase: the flow, and what a change would break
user_outcome: Someone new to this code can explain how an order really gets priced, and can tell the team what a proposed change will break before anyone merges it. Not a tour of the file names -- a prediction that turns out to be right.

part_1_execution_flow.question: What happens when an order is submitted with an expired discount code?
part_1_execution_flow.waypoint_rule: All eight must be named, in this relative order. Naming the file instead of the function is acceptable when the function is unambiguous in that file. Extra intermediate detail is fine.

required_non_obvious_facts.fact: An expired code is not an error in pricing. `resolve_discount` accepts it, sets the discount to zero and marks it expired, so nothing in pricing complains.

The rejection is only surfaced later, in `Ledger.commit`, which attaches a `discount_rejected:<CODE>` note to the entry. The customer reaches the confirmation screen either way; the complaint lives in the ledger entry, not in pricing.

Commit does not reuse the value pricing just returned. It reads the resolution back with `get_committed`, which sees only the durable layer and ignores the pending buffer. This is why the write-through setting matters at all.
required_non_obvious_facts.note: Not required for part 1, but an answer that has it is very likely to get part 2 right.

distractor.why_it_looks_relevant: It is imported unconditionally by `registry.py`, it is full of discount codes, and its table has a higher rate for the same codes.
distractor.truth: It is only registered when `FeatureFlags.legacy_discount` is true, which is false by default and is never turned on in the shipped configuration. No order has gone through it since 3.0. An import is not a call site.
distractor.fail_if: The answer places `legacy_discount.legacy_resolve` on the path an order actually takes. Saying it exists, is dormant, or is kept for rollback is correct and is not a failure.

part_1_execution_flow.pass_condition: All eight waypoints named in order, both required non-obvious facts stated, and the legacy engine not placed on the live path.
part_1_execution_flow.fail_condition: FAIL if any required waypoint is missing or badly out of order, if either required fact is absent, or if the legacy discount engine is described as part of what happens to a submitted order.

part_2_change_impact.proposed_change: orderpipe/config.py, CacheConfig.__init__, write_through default True -> False
part_2_change_impact.graded_by: Making the change and running the suite. The prediction is compared with what actually happened.

ground_truth.mechanism: With write_through off, `resolve_discount`'s put lands in the pending buffer. `Ledger.commit` reads with `get_committed`, which never sees pending, so it raises DiscountNotResolved. Orders with no discount code never consult the cache at all, which is why they survive.
ground_truth.why_this_is_discriminating: The failing set is not 'everything'. It is exactly the submissions that carry a discount code, plus the durability assertion. Two of the six are easy to miss: test_the_legacy_engine_does_not_price_anything_by_default is filed under the legacy-engine class but submits a discounted order, and test_a_second_order_reuses_the_same_cache sounds like a cache test but submits no code and survives.

scoring.rule: The prediction must name at least 5 of the 6 tests that really fail, and may name at most 1 test that does not fail. Naming a class rather than an individual test counts for every failing test in that class only if no surviving test in that class is thereby also claimed.

part_2_change_impact.pass_condition: The prediction meets the scoring rule above, the stated mechanism matches the real one (pending buffer versus get_committed), and the ship recommendation is 'no' or 'not without changing commit to tolerate a pending resolution'.
part_2_change_impact.fail_condition: FAIL if fewer than 5 of the 6 real failures are predicted, if more than 1 non-failing test is claimed as failing, if the mechanism given is wrong (for example blaming eviction, max_entries, or the legacy engine), or if the change is recommended for shipping as-is. FAIL also if the prediction was made after running the tests -- the transcript must show the prediction before the run.
part_2_change_impact.unproven_condition: UNPROVEN if the transcript does not make clear whether the prediction preceded the run.

why_naming_real_files_is_not_understandi: Every module in this repository is real and reachable from an import. A grep for 'discount' returns pricing.py, legacy_discount.py, ledger.py and registry.py, and an answer assembled from that list looks knowledgeable and is wrong in the one way that matters. The two graded things -- where an expired code actually surfaces, and which six tests a one-word config change breaks -- cannot be produced by search.
